title: Retailer Deductions in Q4: How Walmart and Kroger Compare
summary: Retailer deductions hit suppliers differently at Walmart and Kroger, especially in Q4. See how fines and dispute windows compare.
body_markdown:
In this article, learn about:


-


The financial impact of retailer deductions and how much revenue suppliers may be able to recover


-


How Walmart and Kroger calculate penalties for late and short shipments, and why flat fees raise the cost of small mistakes


-


How dispute windows and Q4 volume affect what suppliers recover, and what teams can do before the peak


Retailer deductions don’t have a single cost. The financial impact of a compliance mistake depends on the retailer, the type of deduction, how the retailer calculates the penalty, and how long the supplier has to dispute it.


That matters even more in the fourth quarter. Higher shipment volume, promotions, and ecommerce activity create more opportunities for deductions, while finance and operations teams have the same amount of time to review them.


## How Much Do Retailer Deductions Cost Suppliers?


SPS experts estimate that suppliers lose an average of[2%–10% of annual revenue to recoverable deductions](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/articles/retail-deductions-supplier-playbook-reclaim-lost-revenue) . The range comes from SPS experts rather than an independent industry study, so it works best as a planning range. The range comes from SPS experts rather than an independent industry study, so it works best as a planning range.


SPS estimates also vary by retailer: about 6% of revenue for Amazon suppliers, 5.8% for Walmart suppliers, and 5% for Kroger suppliers. The revenue loss behind each figure varies by supplier.


Two terms are easy to blur, and retailers define them differently. Across the industry, though:


-


A deduction is money a retailer withholds when it pays a supplier’s invoice.


-


A chargeback is an invoice a retailer sends the supplier requesting payment.


In addition, suppliers can face other forms of revenue loss like compliance fines, trade spend, post audits, and overages. SPS uses deductions or revenue loss as the broad term, and this article follows that usage.


**Related Reading:**[Retail Chargeback Costs: What Is a Compliance Cost Curve?](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/articles/retail-chargeback-costs-what-is-a-compliance-cost-curve)


## How Walmart and Kroger Calculate Compliance Penalties


Walmart and Kroger both measure on-time in-full performance, but they use different thresholds and penalty structures. Walmart calls its version the On Time, In Full (OTIF) program. A supplier can have a similar operational problem with both retailers and face different financial consequences.


### Walmart OTIF Chargeback Rate Explained


Walmart’s[OTIF program](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/articles/walmart-otif-metrics) uses separate on-time goals depending on how a shipment moves. Prepaid orders have a 90% on-time goal, while collect orders ready for pickup have a 98% goal. The in-full goal is 95%.


When a supplier misses its goal,[Walmart fines 3% of the cost of goods sold on non-compliant cases](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/articles/holding-3rd-parties-accountable-for-otif-fines) . The fine applies to the cases that failed rather than the entire order, so a shortage on part of a shipment does not turn the whole purchase order (PO) into a 3% penalty.


### Kroger’s Percentage Fines and Flat Fees


Kroger’s ORAD program (Original Requested Arrival Date) policy, updated for 2025,[raised its on-time threshold from 90% to 93% and set the case fill rate at 95%](https://kroger.onenetwork.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/1-VNC-Program-Updates_final_signed.pdf) . When a supplier-caused issue makes a PO arrive late, Kroger fines 3% of the invoiced amount for the whole PO. On a PO filled below 95%, Kroger charges 3% of the value of the missing items. Suppliers that reach 93% on-time delivery over a four-week period owe no late-arrival fees for that period.


Kroger also uses flat fees. The policy lists a $200 fee per shipment that arrives more than 30 minutes after its appointment and a $500 fee per PO for case labeling, case pack, or universal product code (UPC) errors. Some fees do not apply when Kroger manages the inbound freight.


The flat fees change the economics of a deduction. A $500 labeling fee on a $5,000 PO equals 10% of the order value, more than three times the 3% percentage penalty. On smaller orders, the structure of the penalty matters as much as the percentage.

## The Dispute Window Is Part of the Cost


A deduction’s cost includes the time suppliers have to find, support, and dispute it before the retailer’s deadline.


[SPS Commerce research](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/articles/the-impact-of-retailer-deductions) shows that suppliers dispute only 20%–30% of deductions and win back an average of 40% of the deductions they dispute. Dispute windows widen or narrow that gap. Kroger allows 180 days from the original invoice date for billing inquiries. Walmart’s OTIF window depends on the supplier agreement and how Walmart processes the fine.


Walmart’s[OTIF dispute process](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/articles/walmart-otif-dispute-process) also shows why timing matters. Walmart generally issues OTIF fines quarterly, about five weeks after the quarter ends. Once a window closes, the deduction may eliminate the standard opportunity for recovery.


Records get harder to find as invoices age. Proof of delivery, bills of lading, and appointment records are harder to locate weeks or months after a shipment.


## Why Q4 Retailer Compliance Costs Climb


The retailer’s rules usually stay the same during the holiday season, but more shipments, promotions, and online orders create more opportunities for:


-


Late deliveries


-


Short shipments


-


Labeling errors


-


Pricing discrepancies


-


Promotional deductions


-


Ecommerce refunds and fraud


## What Can Supplier Teams Do Before the Peak?


Before the peak, supplier teams can:


-


Track deductions by retailer and reason code each week to spot sudden increases early


-


Compare deduction growth with sales growth for each retailer, since deductions that outpace sales can point to a compliance problem


-


Keep a retailer-specific rulebook with each retailer’s thresholds, penalty basis, measurement period, and dispute window


-


Save proof of delivery, bills of lading, and appointment records for holiday shipments


-


Review open deductions early in the new year, before the post-holiday backlog pushes disputes past a deadline


## Frequently Asked Questions


### What percentage of revenue do suppliers lose to retailer deductions?


SPS experts estimate an average of 2%–10% of annual revenue lost to recoverable deductions, with estimates of about 6% for Amazon suppliers, 5.8% for Walmart suppliers, and 5% for Kroger suppliers. These are SPS expert estimates.


### Are deductions and chargebacks the same thing?


No. The terms mean different things, so suppliers shouldn’t use them interchangeably. Across the industry, a deduction is money a retailer withholds when it pays a supplier’s invoice, and a chargeback is an invoice a retailer sends the supplier requesting payment. Retailers can define the terms differently. Compliance fines, trade spend, post audits, and overages are other forms of revenue loss, so a supplier can face deductions, chargebacks, fines, and more at the same time.


### What is Walmart’s OTIF fine?


Walmart fines 3% of the cost of goods sold on non-compliant cases when a supplier misses its applicable OTIF goal. The goals include 90% on-time for prepaid orders, 98% for collect orders ready for pickup, and 95% in-full.


### How does Kroger’s late-delivery fee work?


Kroger charges 3% of the invoiced amount on a PO that arrives late because of a supplier-caused issue. Suppliers that reach 93% on-time delivery over a four-week period owe no late-arrival fees for that period. Separate flat fees apply to certain appointment, labeling, case-pack, and UPC errors.


### Can suppliers dispute retailer deductions?


Yes. Dispute windows vary by retailer. Kroger allows 180 days from the original invoice date for billing inquiries. Walmart’s OTIF window depends on the supplier agreement and how Walmart processes the fine.


## See Which Retailers Are Driving Your Deductions


Knowing which retailers generate the most deductions only helps if your team can tell why they occurred and which ones are worth disputing.
